newsitem.title: BOSNIA: "Mr No" takes Serb seat in presidency.
newsitem.headline: "Mr No" takes Serb seat in presidency.

text.p: Momcilo Krajisnik, elected on Wednesday to the Serb seat in Bosnia's collective presidency, is an ultra-hardline nationalist who earned the nickname "Mr No" for his uncompromising stand in peace negotiations.

The 52-year-old is the most powerful political figure in the semi-autonomous Serb Republic. He has more clout even than former president Radovan Karadzic, now indicted by the Hague war crimes tribunal.
Krajisnik's strength stems from his control of the police and local authorities, which have led to accusations of war profiteering.
In the 1980s, he spent nine months in prison on embezzlement charges connected with his running of the Yugoslav state company Energoinvest, a Sarajevo-based socialist enterprise.
Later, he said he was persecuted because of his championing of the Serb cause.

Krajisnik, born in Zabrdje near Sarajevo, served as speaker of the assembly in the pre-war Yugoslav republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He resigned when the war began in April 1992 to become speaker of the Bosnian Serb assembly.

Stocky, with thick, dark eyebrows, he is a tenacious negotiator with a reputation for getting his way. His election poses a formidable challenge to the working of the three-man presidency and the wider Dayton peace accords.
Krajisnik was present at every round of peace negotiations before and during the war and never showed any inclination to compromise.
Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic kept him out of the final negotiating sessions at Dayton which -- by its advocacy of a single, unified Bosnian state -- is anathema to the secessionist Krajisnik.

Part of his strength lies in his appeal to the common man. In contrast to other leading figures in the Bosnian Serb leadership, he is not an academic or doctor and before the war he raised pigs and cattle.
